noteRef.topicTitle: 1. Structure, Bonding & Introduction to Organic Chemistry

specPoints.text: understand that covalent bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between two nuclei and the shared pair of electrons between them, based on the evidence: i the physical properties of giant atomic structures ii electron density maps for simple molecules

primer.text: Covalent bonds pool electrons rather than transfer them: two nuclei, one shared pair, stability from a double attraction. Bond polarity grades the sharing by electronegativity difference, and the octet rule bends at both ends - period-3 expansion and boron's deficiency. This note runs from the hydrogen molecule's charge cloud to simple and giant covalent lattices.

lessons.title: Sharing instead of transferring
lessons.opening: Covalent bonding joins two non-metals not by handing electrons over but by holding them together: both nuclei attract the same outer-shell pair, two atomic orbitals overlap into a molecular orbital, and the pair sits more stable in the two-nucleus pull than under one nucleus alone. Drawn as H-H, the bond is best imagined as a moving charge cloud rather than a fixed pair of dots.
keyPoints: Covalent bonding occurs between two non-metal atoms.
The bond is the electrostatic attraction between the two nuclei and their shared outer-shell electrons.
No electrons transfer; they are shared, with two atomic orbitals overlapping into a molecular orbital.
Sharing is stabilising because two nuclei attract the pair more strongly than one nucleus alone.
Bonding electrons are best regarded as constantly moving charge clouds, not fixed positions.

low.restatement: Two non-metals each park an electron into a joint cloud between them; both nuclei tug on that cloud, and the shared tug is what glues the pair together.
low.analogy: Two neighbours each holding one end of the same rope: neither owns it outright, but the shared tension binds them together.
low.examPointer: The one-line definition to memorise: electrostatic attraction between the nuclei and the shared pair of electrons.

medium.restatement: Orbital overlap converts two atomic orbitals into one molecular orbital whose electron density concentrates between the nuclei; the pair's stability rises because each electron now feels the pull of two nuclei at once.
medium.analogy: A hammock slung between two posts sags to its lowest, most comfortable point in the middle - electron density settles between two nuclei the same way.
medium.examPointer: When asked why sharing happens, quote the double attraction: two nuclei on one pair beats one nucleus on one pair.

check.stem: Which atoms combine to form a covalent bond?

options.text: Two non-metals
options.explanation: Sharing electrons suits two atoms that both prefer to gain.

options.text: A metal and a non-metal
options.explanation: That pairing transfers electrons and bonds ionically.

options.text: Two metals
options.explanation: Metallic bonding with delocalised electrons serves that case.

options.text: Any two atoms equally
options.explanation: Bond type follows the partners' electron preferences.

check.stem: What is the electrostatic attraction in a covalent bond between?

options.text: The nuclei of the two atoms and their shared outer-shell electrons
options.explanation: Both nuclei pull on the same pair holding them together.

options.text: Two oppositely charged ions
options.explanation: That describes ionic bonding.

options.text: The electrons of one atom and the neutrons of the other
options.explanation: Neutrons are uncharged and take no part.

options.text: Two pairs of inner-shell electrons
options.explanation: Bonding involves outer-shell electrons.

check.stem: What happens to atomic orbitals when a covalent bond forms?

options.text: They overlap and a molecular orbital forms
options.explanation: The shared arrangement houses the bonding pair.

options.text: They transfer completely to the non-metal atom
options.explanation: No transfer occurs in covalent bonding.

options.text: They annihilate each other
options.explanation: Orbitals combine, never cancel to nothing.

options.text: They remain fully separate
options.explanation: Overlap is the defining event.

check.stem: Why is a shared electron pair more stable than electrons held by a single nucleus?

options.text: Each electron is attracted to two nuclei instead of one
options.explanation: The doubled pull lowers the energy of the pair.

options.text: The electrons repel each other less when shared
options.explanation: Repulsion between the pair is unchanged; the nuclear pull is what changes.

options.text: Sharing removes the electrons entirely
options.explanation: The electrons remain present and shared.

options.text: The nuclei stop repelling when bonding
options.explanation: Nuclear repulsion persists but is overridden by the shared attraction.

check.stem: How should the electrons of a covalent bond be pictured?

options.text: As constantly moving charge clouds rather than fixed positions
options.explanation: The pair roams within the molecular orbital.

options.text: As two dots nailed to fixed points
options.explanation: The fixed-dot picture is a drawing convention, not the physical truth.

options.text: As orbiting planets around one nucleus
options.explanation: The pair belongs to both nuclei at once.

options.text: As a rigid rod between the nuclei
options.explanation: The cloud is diffuse, not rigid.

check.stem: Define the covalent bond in terms of electrostatic attraction.
check.modelAnswer: A covalent bond is the electrostatic pull that binds two nuclei to the shared outer-shell electrons sitting between them.

check.stem: State what is formed when two atomic orbitals overlap.
check.modelAnswer: Overlapping atomic orbitals form a molecular orbital that houses the shared bonding pair.

check.stem: Explain why covalent bonding happens between two non-metals rather than a metal and a non-metal.
check.modelAnswer: Two non-metals both favour gaining electrons, so neither will donate; sharing a pair lets each count the electrons toward a full outer shell without either atom having to give them away.

check.stem: Describe what the H-H bond representation implies about the electrons between the two hydrogen nuclei.
check.modelAnswer: The straight line hides a molecular orbital spanning both nuclei: one electron supplied by each atom forms a shared pair whose charge cloud is spread between and around the two nuclei in constant motion.

lessons.title: Polar bonds and the octet's edges
lessons.opening: Sharing is not always equal. Identical atoms split the pair symmetrically - Cl2 is nonpolar - but a more electronegative partner drags the density its way, giving HCl delta charges and an asymmetric distribution. The eight-electron rule bends at both edges too: period-3 centres expand past eight, and boron centres fall short at six.
keyPoints: Equal electronegativities make a covalent bond nonpolar, as in Cl2.
Different electronegativities make the bond polar, drawing electrons toward the more electronegative atom.
In a polar bond the charge centres do not coincide: the delta-negative and delta-positive ends separate.
The greater the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond, approaching ionic character.
Period-3 atoms can expand past eight electrons; boron compounds can be electron deficient at six.

low.restatement: Identical atoms share fairly; a greedier atom pulls the pair closer, leaving slightly charged ends. Eight electrons is the usual cap, but big atoms can hold more and boron holds fewer.
low.analogy: A tug-of-war between equal teams stays centred; a stronger team drags the rope - and the usual team-size rule bends for giant or short rosters.
low.examPointer: Attach the delta signs correctly: delta-negative sits on the more electronegative atom, delta-positive on the other.

medium.restatement: Polarity is unequal sharing quantified: the electronegativity difference displaces the negative charge centre from the positive one, growing with the difference toward the ionic limit; octet flexibility follows orbital availability - accessible d-orbitals expand period-3 shells, and boron's three valence electrons leave an unfilled orbital.
medium.analogy: A shared blanket pulled by two sleepers of different strength: the stronger one ends up with more blanket, and the 'eight-square' bed rule simply does not fit every sleeper.
medium.examPointer: Quote electron counts for the exceptions: ten around P in PCl5, twelve around S in SF6, six around B in BF3.

check.stem: Why is the bond in Cl2 nonpolar?

options.text: Both chlorine atoms have identical electronegativities, sharing the pair equally
options.explanation: Equal pull keeps the charge centres coincident.

options.text: Chlorine is a metal that transfers electrons
options.explanation: Chlorine is a non-metal that shares.

options.text: The bond is ionic in character
options.explanation: Cl2 is covalent and nonpolar.

options.text: Each atom carries a permanent delta charge
options.explanation: Delta charges appear only in polar bonds.

check.stem: In a polar covalent bond, which atom becomes delta-negative?

options.text: The more electronegative atom
options.explanation: It draws the shared electrons closer to itself.

options.text: The less electronegative atom
options.explanation: It ends up delta-positive.

options.text: The larger atom by mass
options.explanation: Electronegativity, not mass, decides.

options.text: Neither atom
options.explanation: Polarity is defined by the separated partial charges.

check.stem: What happens to a covalent bond as the electronegativity difference grows?

options.text: It becomes more polar, approaching ionic character at the limit
options.explanation: Unequal sharing deepens until transfer takes over.

options.text: It becomes less polar
options.explanation: The difference drives polarity up, not down.

options.text: It stays exactly the same
options.explanation: Polarity scales with the difference.

options.text: It switches polarity direction at midpoint
options.explanation: The more electronegative atom stays delta-negative throughout.

check.stem: Why can phosphorus hold ten electrons around it in PCl5?

options.text: Period-3 atoms can access d-orbitals, expanding beyond eight
options.explanation: The extra orbital space accommodates the tenth electron.

options.text: Phosphorus gains five extra electrons outright
options.explanation: The electrons are shared in bonds, not gained.

options.text: Phosphorus ignores the octet rule entirely
options.explanation: Expansion is the rule's extension, not its abandonment.

options.text: The chlorine atoms hold the extra electrons for it
options.explanation: The count is around the central phosphorus atom.

check.stem: How many electrons surround the central boron atom in BF3, and what is this called?

options.text: Six - an electron-deficient central atom
options.explanation: Three bonds supply six electrons, two short of an octet.

options.text: Eight - a normal octet
options.explanation: BF3 is the classic deficiency example.

options.text: Ten - an expanded octet
options.explanation: Expansion belongs to period-3 atoms like P and S.

options.text: Two - a bare nucleus
options.explanation: Three bonding pairs surround the boron.

check.stem: Define a polar covalent bond.
check.modelAnswer: A polar covalent bond forms between atoms of different electronegativity, drawing the shared electrons toward the more electronegative atom and separating the partial charges.

check.stem: State the electron counts around the central atoms of PCl5, SF6 and BF3.
check.modelAnswer: PCl5 carries ten electrons around phosphorus, SF6 twelve around sulfur, and BF3 six around electron-deficient boron.

check.stem: Explain why the negative and positive charge centres separate in a polar bond.
check.modelAnswer: The shared electron density is pulled asymmetrically toward the more electronegative atom, so the midpoint of negative charge no longer coincides with the positive nuclear centre, leaving delta-negative and delta-positive poles.

check.stem: Predict the polarity of the H-Cl bond, naming the delta assignment on each atom.
check.modelAnswer: Chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen, so the bonding electrons sit closer to Cl, making Cl delta-negative and H delta-positive - a polar bond.

lessons.title: Simple and giant covalent structures
sourceHeadings: Covalent bonding & simple covalent lattice structures
Covalent bonding & giant covalent lattice structures
lessons.opening: The same bond builds two very different worlds. Small molecules - water, nitrogen - hold a fixed atom count and melt easily because only weak intermolecular forces sit between the units. Giant covalent lattices wire countless atoms together with strong covalent bonds, so they melt ferociously high and split into hard diamond-like or soft graphite-like characters depending on where the weak spots sit.
keyPoints: Simple molecules such as H2O and N2 contain fixed numbers of covalently bonded atoms.
Simple covalent lattices melt and boil low because weak intermolecular forces need little energy to break.
Simple covalent compounds rarely conduct: no charged particles exist unless water reaction makes ions, as with HCl.
Giant covalent lattices melt and boil very high because countless strong covalent bonds link the whole structure.
Giant structures can be hard (diamond, silicon(IV) oxide) or soft (graphite, weak between layers).

low.restatement: Little molecules part easily - only weak glue between them - so they melt low and do not conduct. Endless covalent networks take huge energy to break, melting high, and their hardness depends on whether weak layers lurk inside.
low.analogy: A bowl of marbles scatters at a push; a welded steel mesh fights the crowbar - and if the mesh is stacked in slick sheets, it shears soft.
low.examPointer: Conductivity answers hinge on charged particles: name the delocalised electrons in graphite and their absence in diamond.

medium.restatement: Melting temperature reports the weakest link: intermolecular forces for molecular solids, covalent bonds for networks - hence the two regimes differ by hundreds of degrees. Conductivity then demands mobile charge, which molecular solids lack (unless water generates ions) and only layered networks supply.
medium.analogy: Tearing a stack of paper versus sawing a welded frame: the stack fails at its lowest energy path, the frame at its strongest bond.
medium.examPointer: Buckminsterfullerene is the boundary case: a big molecule with high melting points and trapped delocalised electrons that still cannot conduct between molecules.

check.stem: Why do simple covalent lattices have low melting points?

options.text: Only weak intermolecular forces sit between the molecules
options.explanation: Little energy separates the fixed small units.

options.text: Their covalent bonds are weak
options.explanation: The intra-molecular covalent bonds are strong; only the between-molecule forces are weak.

options.text: They contain free ions that shake the lattice
options.explanation: No charged particles exist in simple molecular solids.

options.text: Their molecules are enormous
options.explanation: Simple molecules are small with fixed atom counts.

check.stem: Why does aqueous HCl conduct while pure liquid water-dissolved sucrose solutions of covalent HCl gas differ from solid sugar?

options.text: HCl's interaction with water produces H+ and Cl- ions that carry current
options.explanation: Ion formation in solution grants conductivity to an otherwise covalent compound.

options.text: HCl molecules themselves carry charge
options.explanation: Neutral molecules conduct nothing; the ions do.

options.text: Water always conducts electricity
options.explanation: Pure water is a poor conductor; the ions are what conduct.

options.text: Sugar donates electrons to the water
options.explanation: Sucrose dissolves without ionising.

check.stem: Why is graphite soft but diamond hard?

options.text: Graphite's layers are held by weak forces between them, while diamond's atoms lock into a 3D covalent network
options.explanation: Weak interlayer forces shear easily; the tetrahedral network resists.

options.text: Graphite's covalent bonds are weaker than diamond's
options.explanation: Within the layers the bonds are very strong.

options.text: Diamond contains intermolecular forces that stiffen it
options.explanation: Diamond has no intermolecular forces at all.

options.text: Both are equally hard
options.explanation: Their structures differ sharply in shear behaviour.

check.stem: Why does graphite conduct electricity but diamond does not?

options.text: Graphite keeps one delocalised electron per atom that travels along the layers
options.explanation: Three of four outer electrons bond; the fourth roams.

options.text: Diamond's electrons are delocalised in all directions
options.explanation: All four of diamond's outer electrons sit in covalent bonds.

options.text: Graphite ions migrate under voltage
options.explanation: No ions exist in graphite.

options.text: Diamond's bonds block all electron motion entirely
options.explanation: Its electrons are local in bonds; that is the reason, correctly framed.

check.stem: Buckminsterfullerene, C60, differs from typical simple molecules because

options.text: its large spherical network gives stronger intermolecular forces and higher melting points, though it is not giant covalent
options.explanation: More electrons mean bigger dispersion forces, yet the structure stays molecular.

options.text: it is classed as a giant covalent structure
options.explanation: Fullerenes are explicitly not giant covalent.

options.text: it conducts electricity well through its delocalised electrons
options.explanation: The electrons cannot pass between molecules.

options.text: it melts lower than any small molecule
options.explanation: It melts higher, thanks to size.

check.stem: State the two structure classes covalent bonding produces, with one example each.
check.modelAnswer: Simple molecular structures (H2O, N2) and giant covalent lattices (diamond, graphite) - fixed small units versus endless bonded networks.

check.stem: State the melting-point character of simple covalent lattices and giant covalent lattices.
check.modelAnswer: Simple covalent lattices melt and boil low; giant covalent lattices melt and boil very high.

check.stem: Explain why most covalent compounds fail to conduct in any state.
check.modelAnswer: Conduction needs mobile charged particles; simple molecular solids and liquids contain neutral molecules with no free ions or electrons, so nothing can carry current unless reaction with water manufactures ions.

check.stem: Sort SiO2, N2, graphite and C60 by melting-point character and give each one's structural reason.
check.modelAnswer: Highest: SiO2 (giant covalent network); then C60 (large molecule, strong intermolecular forces); then N2 (tiny molecule, weak forces); graphite sits with the networks at very high melting despite its shearable layers.

glossary.definition: The combined orbital formed when two atomic orbitals overlap in a covalent bond, housing the shared pair.
The region of constantly moving electron density that represents a bonding pair.
A covalent bond between atoms of different electronegativity whose shared electrons sit closer to one atom, giving delta charges.
Describing a central atom with fewer than eight outer electrons, such as boron in BF3.
